transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
President Trump's meeting with China, Xi Jinping,
and Russia's Vladimir Putin today in China has wrapped up
in the first trilateral summit between the three.
They are two of America's leading rivals.
Trump says the leaders have a special responsibility
to maintain communications with each other,
focusing on nuclear weapons.
As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far,
the United States, Russia, and China uniquely positioned
to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons
on Earth and also to lessen the risk
that those weapons will ever be used.
The power is unbelievable, unthinkable.
Putin says Russia, China, and the U.S.
can strengthen global stability
if they cooperate constructively.
Xi says relations between the U.S. and China
have been "generally stable and improved"
during Trump's presidency, but he says the two countries
have to improve communications and trade issues.
Ahead of this three-way meeting,
Trump met individually with both Xi and Putin.
Meanwhile, while China greeted President Trump
and other world leaders with pomp and fanfare,
a key U.S. ally got a different kind of welcome.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn has more.
Unlike President Trump's elaborate welcome,
Japan's Prime Minister, Senaya Takeuchi,
was greeted by no high-level officials,
large honor guard, or crowds of flag-waving youths.
She later shook hands with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice,
but they held no meeting.
Ties between Beijing and Tokyo have been in the deep freeze
since Takeuchi said a year ago
that a naval blockade of Taiwan
could warrant a Japanese military response.
Some Japanese felt that Takeuchi was treated rudely
as punishment for her comments.
Others are concerned that Trump may side with Russia and China
without regard for Japan's interests.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
Officials in Texas have identified a man fatally shot
by a U.S. Border Patrol agent in Laredo earlier this month
as 44-year-old Ernesto Quintina of Laredo.
Texas Public Radio's Diego Medel has more.
The Texas Department of Public Safety
says Border Patrol agents
approached Quintana's vehicle in Laredo
in the early hours of November 2nd
as part of a human smuggling investigation.
Investigators say Quintana accelerated a way,
striking and injuring one agent
before another agent opened fire, killing him.
Five people suspected of being in the country illegally
were taken into custody following the shooting.
According to his obituary,
Quintana was a lifelong Laredo resident and a father of six.
The Texas Rangers are leading the investigation
at the request of federal authorities.
DPS says no state troopers were involved in the shooting.
I'm Diego Medel in San Antonio.
While financial markets, Asian markets,
ended the day in mixed territory,
the Nikkei in Japan up 7/10 of a percent,
the Hang Seng in Hong Kong down nearly 2%.
You're listening to NPR News.
A string of recent tech outages has cut off access
to email, bank accounts, and other everyday services.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports experts say a backup plan
can help when systems suddenly go down.
Most of the recent disruptions were outages
rather than data breaches.
Lori Crainer of Carnegie Mellon University
says the problems exposed how dependent people have become
on a small number of services.
For a bank account, you have another bank account
at another bank where you can at least access cash
or a credit card so that if you can't access money
from one bank, there's another place.
Crainer recommends the same kind of backup for communication.
That can mean keeping a second email account
with a different provider and making sure text messages
don't depend on the same system.
She says important files should also be saved
on a personal device instead of only in the cloud.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is meeting EU officials
in Brussels tomorrow to talk about closer ties
between the UK and the bloc it left in 2020.
Burnham wants to undo what he says is the damage
caused by Brexit, suggesting that rejoining the EU
is a possibility.
That's a shift from the previous silence
of British governments on reversing Brexit.
Economists say it's hurt the UK economy,
but politicians have been cautious
about reopening the debate.
The summit is the second since the UK left the EU.
I'm Janine Hurst, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Trump, Xi, and Putin hold first trilateral summit in China focused on nuclear weapons
Japan's PM Takeuchi receives cold welcome in China amid frozen Beijing-Tokyo ties
Texas officials identify Laredo man Ernesto Quintana, killed by Border Patrol agent
Recent tech outages prompt experts to recommend backup email, banking, and file storage
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham to meet EU officials in Brussels on closer ties
